lesson.title: Turning Up the Heat: Why a Few Degrees Change So Much
lesson.summary: Reaction rates are unusually sensitive to temperature because the fraction of molecules with enough energy to react grows exponentially, not gently, as temperature rises, a direct consequence of the Arrhenius equation.
lesson.body:
Collision theory says a reaction's rate depends on three things: how often molecules collide (collision frequency), what fraction of those collisions are oriented correctly (the orientation factor), and what fraction have enough energy to clear the activation barrier. Raising the temperature affects all three, but not equally. Collision frequency increases only mildly with temperature, since average molecular speed scales with the square root of absolute temperature; going from 300 K to 310 K increases speeds, and therefore collision frequency, by only a few percent. The orientation factor does not depend on temperature at all, since it is a matter of geometry, not motion. It is the third piece, the fraction of collisions with energy at or above Ea, that responds violently to temperature, because that fraction is set by the exponential term in the Arrhenius equation, e^(-Ea/RT), and exponential functions are famously sensitive to small changes in their exponent.

Let's put a real number on that sensitivity. Take the reaction from the Arrhenius Plot chapter, which had an activation energy of 53.6 kJ/mol (53,600 J/mol). What fraction of molecules have at least this much energy at room temperature, 300 K?

f = e^(-Ea/RT) = e^(-53,600 / (8.314 * 300)) = e^(-53,600 / 2,494.2) = e^(-21.49) = 4.6 x 10^-10

That is an extraordinarily small fraction, fewer than one in a billion. At any instant, the overwhelming majority of molecules in a room-temperature sample simply do not have enough energy to react, no matter how often they collide. This is exactly why so many reactions that are thermodynamically favorable, meaning they release energy overall, still sit around at room temperature without visibly happening: the activation barrier keeps almost everyone out.

Now raise the temperature by just 10 degrees, to 310 K, and recompute:

f = e^(-53,600 / (8.314 * 310)) = e^(-53,600 / 2,577.3) = e^(-20.79) = 9.3 x 10^-10

The fraction of sufficiently energetic molecules has roughly doubled, from about 4.6 x 10^-10 to about 9.3 x 10^-10, for a temperature change of just 10 K, about a 3 percent change in absolute temperature. Since collision frequency and orientation barely moved over that same 10 degree span, essentially the entire doubling of the reaction rate comes from this one exponential term. That is precisely the doubling you already saw show up as the doubled rate constant in the Arrhenius Plot chapter's worked example (k going from 3.0 x 10^-4 to 6.0 x 10^-4 per second between the same two temperatures); this chapter shows you the molecular reason behind that number.

This exponential sensitivity is the reason temperature control matters so much in chemistry and in everyday life. It is why food spoils far faster on a warm counter than in a cold refrigerator, why a fever of even a couple of degrees can meaningfully speed up or disrupt the enzyme-catalyzed reactions running inside the human body, and why chemists running a synthesis in the lab will often care about controlling temperature to within a degree or two: a reaction is never linearly sensitive to temperature, it is exponentially sensitive, and the Arrhenius equation is what lets you calculate exactly how much.
